enablement.action: apply the brand's look and wording correctly on your own

guidance.claim: Brand values and purpose belong in the Product Vision and the Positioning Statement. Ask whether a passage says what the brand stands for (put it there) or how the brand should feel and be expressed in look and wording (keep it here).
Brand guidelines, a brand book and a style guide all count as this guide when they set the brand's intended feeling and its rules for look and wording, whatever the document is called.
DESIGN.md represents visual design-system rules. It can supply the visual portion of a brand guide; it does not represent its verbal rules.
Instructions for revising the document are not part of the document. That is a process, and it belongs wherever the process is owned.
Stale when an adopted colour, typeface, logo or other brand asset changes. A guide that shows a look nobody uses any more misleads more confidently than having no guide.
The opening Overview of a DESIGN.md carries this: personality, audience and the response the brand should evoke. It is what to fall back on when no rule covers a case.

sections.name: Brand character
sections.question: What feeling should the brand's look and wording create?

guidance.claim: Distinct from Verbal Identity Rules: marks, colour, type and imagery, and how the name is drawn as a logotype, are look; words, voice, naming, standing copy, and how the name is spelled, cased and punctuated in text, are wording. A trademark policy usually splits across both.
A rule set with nothing forbidden is usually not settled yet.
Mood boards help a team agree on a feeling before any rule exists, and get copied into the rules by mistake. Record only what was adopted: the final colours, type and marks.
The machine-readable form fixes the order the sections come in, and requires none of them except a primary colour palette.
Token formats carry colour, size, type and timing. Icons, accessibility and writing rules fit in none of them, and are no less settled for that.
Name a specific reference rather than a list of adjectives. 'Modern, clean, premium' fits almost anything.

Distinct from Cross-Cutting Concerns: here go the brand's standing rules for its look; a record that one design meets an obligation such as accessibility goes there. Ask whether the line sets a rule for all material or checks one piece of work.
Most of these are only partly answered. A settled palette and nothing else is a real answer, not a stub.

sections.name: Visual identity rules
sections.question: What are the rules for the brand's look?

guidance.claim: Writing sits among the foundations as a peer of colour and typography, not beneath them.
Where the guide is split into a visual branch and a content or messaging branch, as GitLab's Pajamas is, put these rules in the content branch.
The words a brand refuses do as much work as the ones it adopts.

Distinct from Positioning Statement and Value Proposition: here goes the approved wording itself, such as boilerplate, taglines and pitches of set lengths. Ask whether you are fixing words or deciding what to claim; deciding what to claim belongs there, and the wording here draws on it without restating it.
Where wording is decided case by case and no rules exist, note that here, so a reader can tell it apart from rules that exist but have not been collected.

sections.name: Verbal identity rules
sections.question: What are the rules for the brand's wording?

guidance.claim: For [segment] who [need], X is a [category] that [benefit], unlike [alternative].
Brand-led organisations treat this as marketing's asset and product-led ones as product's. Settle ownership before it gets written twice.
Pre-competition work often cannot fill the 'unlike' clause honestly. Leave it empty rather than fake it.

sections.name: Positioning statement
sections.question: Which kind of offering should each segment see ours as?

guidance.claim: Imposed, not chosen: regulation, budget, deadline, platform, physics.

Distinct from Cross-Cutting Concerns: a constraint is an imposed limit on the work that no design choice moves — budget, deadline, platform, what the law allows; a cross-cutting concern is an obligation every part of the solution must be designed to meet — security, privacy, accessibility. One law can supply both: a limit here, a property demanded throughout there.
Distinct from Trade-offs. Mislabelling a choice as a constraint hides a decision.

sections.name: Constraints
sections.question: What imposed limits apply to the work?

guidance.claim: Each wants an owner and a resolution path. An unowned question is a risk mislabelled.

Distinct from Risks & Assumptions: an open question is something to answer before a point can be settled; an assumption is a belief the work proceeds on and checks along the way. Proceeding without the answer turns the question into an assumption.
Compare the list across drafts: it should get shorter. A list that keeps growing means the work is not yet ready to settle.
Write 'none open' only when every question raised has been answered or recorded as an assumption, so a reader can tell it apart from a list nobody has drawn up.
